newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - FOMC meeting, housing starts.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - FOMC meeting, housing starts.

text.p: A Federal Reserve policy meeting and the July housing starts report are the standout features of the U.S. government securities trading session on Tuesday, analysts said.
There is little doubt, however, about the outcome of the Fed policy meeting.

Fed watchers polled by Reuters unanimously said that the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the policy-making arm of the Fed, would leave monetary policy unchanged at its Tuesday meeting, neither raising nor lowering interest rates.
The July housing starts report, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, could stir a little more excitement if it deviates substantially from expectations.

Economists polled by Reuters on Friday estimated, on average, that housing starts totaled 1.46 million on an annualized, seasonally adjusted basis in July, narrowly higher than the June rate of 1.452 million.
The economists said lower mortgage rates in July, improved consumer confidence and weather more suitable to outdoor construction activity, led to the increase in starts.

A government report on July import and export prices due at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT is not expected to affect the market, analysts said. In June, import prices rose 0.4 percent while export prices edged down 0.1 percent. Forecasts for July import and export price trends were not available.
The weekly BTM/Schroder and Lynch, Jones & Ryan Redbook reports are two items that sometimes move the market.

The BTM/Schroder report on department and chain store sales officially is released at 0900 EDT/1300 GMT. But the number typically is rumored in the market before that time and can affect the market's early tone.

The Redbook department and chain store sales report's official release time is 1455 EDT/1855 GMT. Last week, government securities prices gave up ground after the Redbook report revealed a stronger-than-expected 0.9 percent sales gain for the week ended August 9.
"The housing starts number will be important only if it offers a surprise in any direction," said Michael Moran chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
Moran said that while the consensus forecast is for a slight increase in starts, he expects a mild decrease.

"Last June we had a high level of multi-family starts and we think that will correct itself this month," he said. "But at the same time, we had low interest rates and good home sales so some analysts look for strong single-family starts."
Moran said the July import and export price report could also offer some insights -- especially the import prices.

"Import prices have helped our favorable inflation results," said Morna. "You can get clues from this series about what is happening with foreign competition and draw inferences about what might happen to the tone of our inflation situation in the future."
Moran said non-petroleum import prices have been declining rather consistently over the past year and a half. In June, they rose 0.2 percent.
"It will be interesting to see what happened in July, to see whether the June increase was just an aberration or if we are starting to see some upward pressure from import prices."
Moran agreed with other analysts that the FOMC meeting would be uneventful.

"I cannot imagine the Fed tightening at Tuesday's meeting," he said. "It would subject them to such an avalanche of criticism. They could not defend a move now. The inflation numbers have been well behaved. But even more significantly, economic growth has been moderate."
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew at a 2.2 percent rate in the second quarter, the government has reported.
The Fed's own industrial production data showed that manufacturing output rose just 0.1 percent in July.
July retail sales were up, but not vigorous, said Moran.
Even the July employment report did not imply strong economic growth, he contended.

"There was a big payroll increase but there was a drop in the length of the average workweek, telling you that new workers were being used to ease the burden on existing employees rather than to increase production," said Moran.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond closed at 98-2/32, up 10/32, to yield 6.52 percent.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open between 5-7/16 percent and 5-1/2 percent on Tuesday.
